summary.text: For \(k=31\) and \(s=1\), the sums at \(n=5\) and \(n=1829=31\cdot59\) are both \(17/288\): indeed, \(1/62+1/1860=1/60\) and \(1/60+1/90=1/36\), leaving \(1/32+1/36\) in each case. Hence the distinct inputs \(5\) and \(1829\) have equal fractional parts.

full_proof.text:
For positive integers \(n,k,s\), write
\[
S_{k,s}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{1}{(d+k)^s},
\]
where the sum is over the positive divisors of \(n\). The conjecture asserts, in particular, that for every fixed pair of positive integers \(k,s\), the fractional parts of the values \(S_{k,s}(n)\) are pairwise distinct as \(n\) ranges over the positive integers. We disprove this assertion by taking
\[
k=31,\qquad s=1,
\]
and exhibiting the two distinct positive integers
\[
n_1=5,
\qquad
n_2=1829.
\]
In fact, the corresponding sums are equal as rational numbers, which is stronger than merely having equal fractional parts.

First consider \(n_1=5\). Since \(5\) is prime, its positive divisors are exactly \(1\) and \(5\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(5)
 &=\sum_{d\mid 5}\frac1{d+31}\\
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{5+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the common denominator \(288\), this is
\[
S_{31,1}(5)=\frac9{288}+\frac8{288}=\frac{17}{288}.
\]

Now factor the second integer:
\[
1829=31\cdot 59.
\]
Both factors are prime and they are distinct. Indeed, to check that \(31\) is prime it suffices to test prime divisors not exceeding \(\sqrt{31}<6\), namely \(2,3,5\), and none divides \(31\). Similarly, \(\sqrt{59}<8\), and none of \(2,3,5,7\) divides \(59\), so \(59\) is prime. Consequently the positive divisors of \(1829=31\cdot59\) are exactly
\[
1,\ 31,\ 59,\ 31\cdot59=1829.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(1829)
 &=\sum_{d\mid1829}\frac1{d+31}\\
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{31+31}
   +\frac1{59+31}+\frac1{1829+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last three terms combine to \(1/36\). Explicitly, \(5580\) is a common denominator, and
\[
\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}
 =\frac{90}{5580}+\frac{62}{5580}+\frac3{5580}
 =\frac{155}{5580}
 =\frac1{36}.
\]
It follows that
\[
S_{31,1}(1829)
 =\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}
 =\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{31,1}(5)=S_{31,1}(1829)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Equal rational numbers necessarily have equal fractional parts. In fact, because \(0<17/288<1\), the fractional part of each of these two sums is itself \(17/288\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{frac}\bigl(S_{31,1}(5)\bigr)
=
\operatorname{frac}\bigl(S_{31,1}(1829)\bigr).
\]
But \(5\ne1829\), while both indices are positive, and \(k=31\) and \(s=1\) are also positive. Thus, for the fixed positive parameters \((k,s)=(31,1)\), two distinct positive indices give the same fractional part. This directly contradicts the conjectured pairwise distinctness.

The conjecture is a conjunction of pairwise distinctness and the additional assertion that none of the sums is an integer. A failure of the pairwise-distinctness clause alone suffices to falsify the whole conjecture. Therefore the stated generalized conjecture is false.
